screens.title: Cache Coherence Basics and Snooping
screens.narratorSegment: In multiprocessor systems each core often keeps its own private cache to reduce latency. That speed comes with a coordination cost: if two cores cache the same memory location, a write by one can leave the other holding stale data. This is the cache coherence problem. In this chapter you will learn how snooping protocols use a shared broadcast network to let caches observe requests, how the MSI and MESI state machines control ownership and sharing, and why directory approaches replace broadcasts for larger systems. We'll also look at practical extensions like MOESI and MESIF and a brief hands-on simulation you can run. The goal is practical: you should be able to explain why a read-then-write pattern causes extra bus traffic in MSI and how MESI removes that cost using the Exclusive state. You'll also learn when snooping is an efficient design and when directory bookkeeping becomes necessary. Notice how all these mechanisms trade off bus bandwidth, latency, and hardware complexity. As you move through the lesson, imagine two people reading the same book: when one rewrites a page, the other must learn about the change or discard the page. That simple analogy will guide the concrete protocols we cover and prepare you to reason about scalability and hybrid designs.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Overview
Cache Coherence Basics and Snooping
Understand conflicts, protocols, and when broadcasts fail to scale.

This chapter focuses on the coherence problem in shared-memory multiprocessors and practical solutions. We'll start with the simple MSI snooping protocol, extend it to MESI, note further enhancements like MOESI and MESIF, and finish with directory-based approaches for scalability.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Concept Map
Caches act like independent book readers; coherence protocols are the rules and messages that keep pages aligned. Snooping uses broadcasts, directories use a librarian lookup.
Protocol Highlights
  • MSI: simple snoop states (M, S, I)

  • Directory: scales with point-to-point messages

screens.title: The Cache Coherence Problem
screens.narratorSegment: Cache coherence is the property that all processors observe a consistent value for a memory location as if memory were a single shared store. The problem arises when private caches allow one core to modify a value while other cores keep older cached copies. Consider two cores, P1 and P2, both caching address A. If P1 writes A = 5 into its cache and does not update memory immediately, P2 may still have the old value 0 and read stale data. That mismatch breaks the expectation that reads reflect the most recent write. Coherence protocols solve this by defining states and messages so caches either invalidate stale copies or supply the new value. Practically, a protocol must handle three events: a processor read when its line is invalid, a processor write when others may have copies, and requests from other caches for the latest value. A common misconception is to equate coherence with consistency: coherence ensures updates to a single location are propagated, whereas consistency defines the ordering seen across multiple locations. Another misconception is assuming hardware automatically keeps caches synchronized without explicit protocol traffic—snooping or directory messages are the mechanism that enforces correctness. To check your understanding, imagine a read-after-write by different cores; can you explain which cache supplies data and which copies are invalidated? The core insight is that coherence enforces a per-location agreement through state transitions and communication.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Coherence ensures all caches agree about the value of each memory location after writes, using state and message rules to avoid stale reads.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › The Cache Coherence Problem
Problem statement
Multiple private caches can hold different values for the same address; coherence enforces agreement.
Concrete example
P1 writes A=5 into its cache. P2 still has A=0. If P2 reads, it sees stale data. A coherence protocol must prevent or correct this.
Why it matters
Correct program behavior and reproducibility depend on a coherent view of memory across cores. Without it, shared-memory algorithms break.
Common misconception
Coherence is not the same as consistency. Coherence is per-location agreement; consistency governs ordering across locations. Also, hardware does not magically keep caches synchronized without protocol traffic.
Analogy
Two people reading the same book: if one edits a page, the other must be told or discard the page; otherwise they read different stories.
Check your understanding
If a processor writes and keeps the line Modified, what should happen when another cache issues a read for that line?
Key Takeaway

Coherence requires protocol actions to keep cached copies consistent; without it shared-memory semantics fail.

screens.title: Snooping Protocols and Bus Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: Snooping protocols rely on a shared broadcast medium so every cache can observe memory requests and act accordingly. The basic bus transactions you must know are BusRd, BusRdX (read-exclusive), and sometimes BusUpgr (upgrade). When a cache sees a BusRd for a block it holds in Modified state, it must either write the modified data back to memory or forward the data to the requester, then downgrade to Shared. If it holds the block in Shared state, it stays Shared and does not need to write back. On a BusRdX, caches with Shared or Modified copies must invalidate their copies. The typical flow for a processor Read in an Invalid state is: issue BusRd, other caches snoop, if someone has Modified they supply data and become Shared; otherwise memory provides the data. For a processor Write in Invalid or Shared, the cache issues BusRdX or BusUpgr; other caches invalidate. A common misconception is that snooping means immediate coherence at zero cost. In fact, snooping requires every cache to inspect every broadcast, consuming interconnect bandwidth and power. This is why snooping is most effective on small systems with an ordered bus. To practice, trace a Read then Write sequence and mark exact bus events and state transitions; you will see why BusRdX and BusUpgr differ in cost.

keyIdea.title: Snooping summary
keyIdea.text: Snooping broadcasts let caches observe requests; BusRd, BusRdX, and BusUpgr are the key transactions that drive state changes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Snooping Protocols
Snooping flow
  1. PrRd when line is I: issue BusRd. If another cache is M, it supplies data and becomes S; requester becomes S.
  2. PrWr when line is S or I: issue BusRdX or BusUpgr to invalidate others; requester moves to M.
  3. BusRd seen by M holder: supply data or write back, then downgrade to S.
Practical note
Snooping requires all caches to snoop every broadcast. That's simple and fast on a small shared bus but saturates as core counts grow.
Transaction quick reference
BusRd — request to read a block; other caches may supply the data if M.
BusRdX — request exclusive ownership for writing; others invalidate.
BusUpgr — upgrade from S to M when the requester already holds the block; avoids data transfer.
Key Takeaway

Snooping uses broadcast transactions that are simple but consume bandwidth; count BusRd and BusRdX to measure cost.

screens.title: MSI Protocol: States and Transitions
screens.narratorSegment: MSI is the simplest common snooping coherence protocol. Each cache line is in exactly one of three states: Modified means the cache has the only valid copy and it differs from memory; Shared means the line is clean and one or more caches may hold it; Invalid means the cache has no valid copy. The protocol defines transitions on processor and bus events. For example, a processor read when the line is Invalid issues a BusRd; if another cache has Modified it supplies data and becomes Shared. The requester moves to Shared. A processor write when the line is Shared must invalidate other copies by issuing BusRdX, and then the requester moves to Modified. If a cache in Modified observes a BusRd for its line it must write the updated data back or forward it and downgrade to Shared. A common confusion is the difference between BusRd and BusRdX: BusRd asks for data for reading, while BusRdX asks for exclusive permission to modify, prompting invalidations. Another subtle point is BusUpgr, which upgrades S to M without data transfer when the requester already holds the line. To build intuition, trace specific sequences and annotate which cache supplies data and which transitions occur; this trains you to count writes back to memory and to reason about latency impact.

keyIdea.title: MSI nutshell
keyIdea.text: MSI uses M, S, and I states to ensure a single writer and correct sharing, with bus transactions driving transitions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › MSI: States & Transitions
States
Modified (M) — only this cache has the updated copy; memory is stale.
Shared (S) — clean copy; may be present in multiple caches.
Invalid (I) — no valid copy.
Key transitions
  • PrRd on I → BusRd → become S (or E in MESI).
  • PrWr on S → BusRdX/BusUpgr → become M after invalidations.
  • BusRd seen by M → supply data, M → S.
Annotated transition table
Event: PrRd
If I: BusRd issued. If another cache is M, that cache supplies data and moves to S. Requester → S.
Event: PrWr
If S: issue BusRdX to invalidate others, then move to M. If I: fetch then invalidate, then M.
Event: BusRd
If you are M: supply data and downgrade to S. If S: remain S. If I: ignore.
Event: BusRdX
If you are M or S: invalidate (→ I). If M: write back first.
Key Takeaway

MSI enforces a single writer (M) and allows multiple readers (S); bus events implement the necessary communication.

screens.title: Simulating MSI: Python Trace Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: A small simulator helps make MSI behavior concrete. The hands-on activity asks you to implement caches with three states per line and model BusRd and BusRdX transactions. The given sequence exercises reads and writes and illustrates invalidations and data supply. Conceptually, implement each cache as an array of lines storing state and data. On a processor read when the line is invalid, issue a BusRd and let any M holder supply data then downgrade to S. On a processor write, issue BusRdX; other S holders transition to I, and any M holder writes back then invalidates. A common error is forgetting to downgrade M to S on a BusRd and thus failing to supply the latest value. The example sequence to trace is: P1 Read 0; P2 Read 0; P1 Write 0; P2 Read 0; P2 Write 0; P1 Read 0. When you run the simulator, after P1's write the line should be M in P1 and I in P2; when P2 later reads, it should see the latest value supplied by P1 or memory and transition to S. Extending the simulator to MESI demonstrates how Exclusive avoids a BusRdX for read-then-write when no other cache holds the line. Implement the code, run the trace, and annotate each step with state changes.

keyIdea.title: Simulation goal
keyIdea.text: Model per-line M, S, I states, BusRd and BusRdX, and trace the example sequence to observe state changes and data flow.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › MSI Simulator
Simulator sketch (Python)
# Simplified simulator sketch
caches = { 'P1': [{'state':'I','data':0} for _ in range(4)],
           'P2': [{'state':'I','data':0} for _ in range(4)] }

# Sequence: P1:Read0, P2:Read0, P1:Write0, P2:Read0, P2:Write0, P1:Read0
# Implement handlers: proc_read(cpu, addr), proc_write(cpu, addr, value)
# Each handler issues BusRd or BusRdX and snoops other caches to update states.
You should fill in the bus logic: when BusRd is issued, check for M holders to supply data and downgrade to S; when BusRdX is issued, invalidate S holders and write-back M if present.
Trace checklist
  • After P1 Read 0: P1: S, P2: I
  • After P2 Read 0: P1: S, P2: S
  • After P1 Write 0: P1: M, P2: I
  • After P2 Read 0: P1 supplies data, both move to S or P1 stays M and supplies then downgrades to S depending on protocol.
Common mistake
Not implementing data supply from an M holder on BusRd leads to reading stale memory instead of the latest cached value.
Key Takeaway

A simulator makes explicit who supplies data and when lines are invalidated; this clarifies protocol costs and behavior.

screens.title: MESI: Introducing the Exclusive State
screens.narratorSegment: MESI extends MSI with an Exclusive (E) state. The E state means a cache has the line, it matches memory, and no other cache holds it. That simple fact yields a meaningful optimization: if a processor reads a line and no other cache has it, the line enters E rather than S. Later, if the processor wants to write to that same line, it can transition directly to Modified without issuing BusRdX because it already knows it is the sole holder. This avoids an extra broadcast and invalidation when the common pattern is read-then-write by the same core. A concrete example: a thread reads a private variable then writes to it; under MSI the read yields S and a subsequent write issues BusRdX even though no other cache has the line, incurring unnecessary bus traffic. MESI prevents that. A typical misconception is thinking Exclusive implies the line is modified; E is clean but exclusive. Also, MESI requires the bus to detect sharers: when a BusRd occurs, caches must confirm whether they have a copy, so the requester can be granted E if no sharers respond. The main trade-off is slightly more complex state logic in exchange for reduced bus events on common read-then-write sequences. Try converting the MSI simulator to MESI and observe fewer BusRdX events in traces where reads are followed by writes by the same core.

keyIdea.title: MESI advantage
keyIdea.text: Exclusive allows a read to promise sole ownership, enabling a later write without an extra invalidation broadcast.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › MESI: Exclusive
E state meaning
Exclusive means an unmodified copy owned solely by this cache. It allows a subsequent write without a BusRdX, saving broadcast traffic in the common read-then-write case.
When a PrRd finds no sharers, transition to E instead of S.
PrWr from E → M with no bus transaction: write locally and mark Modified.
Concrete contrast
MSI: Read→S then Write→BusRdX. MESI: Read→E then Write→M (no BusRdX). Observe reduced bus traffic for read-then-write by a single core.
Key Takeaway

Exclusive gives a cheap local write after a solo read, lowering bus transactions for a common pattern.

screens.title: MOESI and MESIF: Owned and Forward States
screens.narratorSegment: MOESI and MESIF add additional states to optimize communication. MOESI introduces Owned (O), which represents a dirty copy that may be shared: the owning cache supplies the modified data to requesters without immediately writing back to memory. This avoids extra writebacks when multiple caches read a dirty block; ownership lets one cache remain responsible for coherence while others hold read-only access. MESIF introduces Forward (F), a clean-state optimization where one cache is designated to forward data to others, reducing duplicate responses to a BusRd. Practically, these states reduce memory traffic and duplicate cache responses but add complexity: you must track an owner or a forwarder and ensure the right cache responds on a bus read. A common misconception is that more states always improve performance; in practice the gains depend on workload: write-heavy sharing patterns may benefit from Owned, while read-heavy patterns can leverage Forward to reduce memory accesses. When extending a simulator, add ownership and forwarder bookkeeping, and test workloads that perform many read sharers or frequent dirty sharing to measure benefit. The core takeaways are trade-offs: more states mean more hardware logic but can save latency and memory bandwidth in the right scenarios.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › MOESI & MESIF
MOESI — Owned
A cache in Owned has the latest data and can supply it to others; memory may be stale. This avoids immediate writebacks on sharing of dirty data.
MESIF — Forward
One cache is marked Forward so it responds to BusRd requests for clean data, reducing duplicate responses and memory accesses.

Extensions trade hardware complexity for reduced memory traffic and fewer writebacks under specific sharing patterns.

screens.title: Directory-Based Coherence
screens.narratorSegment: Directory-based coherence moves bookkeeping to a directory (often distributed at memory controllers) that tracks which caches hold each memory block. A directory entry typically records the block state (uncached, shared, modified), a sharer bit vector, and an optional owner for Modified blocks. When a cache wants to read or write, it sends a request to the directory. The directory looks up the sharers and forwards requests only to those caches that have copies. This avoids broadcasting to all caches and thus scales much better as core counts grow. For example, if only two of a hundred cores share a block, the directory will contact only those two instead of broadcasting to all one hundred. A common misconception is thinking directories eliminate all latency; they reduce bandwidth but add directory lookup latency and storage overhead. Another subtlety is directory storage: maintaining a full bit vector per block requires space that can be significant at very large scales, so directory implementations use optimizations like limited sharer lists or coarse-grain tracking. The trade-offs are clear: directory protocols use more complex metadata and slightly higher latency per request but avoid the heavy broadcast costs that make snooping impractical beyond small systems.

Directory entry
State: Uncached / Shared / Modified
Sharers: Bit vector or list of caches holding the block in Shared state
Owner: The cache holding Modified data, if any
When a cache requests a block, the directory issues targeted messages: invalidate only the known sharers or ask the owner to write back. This reduces broadcast traffic at the cost of directory storage and lookup latency.
Concrete example
If only caches A and B hold a block among 128 cores, the directory contacts only A and B rather than broadcasting to all cores.
Trade-off
Lower broadcast bandwidth versus added directory storage and lookup latency.

screens.title: Snooping vs Directory: Trade-offs and Scalability
screens.narratorSegment: Snooping and directory protocols trade simplicity and low latency for scalability and reduced broadcast cost. Snooping is simple: every cache listens to a shared bus and reacts immediately. This yields low-latency coherence actions in small systems and simpler state machines. However, snooping's cost grows with the number of cores because every broadcast must be snooped by every cache, consuming bandwidth and power. Directory-based coherence avoids full broadcasts by maintaining per-block sharer information and sending targeted point-to-point messages only to relevant caches. That scales to tens, hundreds, or thousands of cores but introduces directory lookup latency and hardware to store and manage sharer lists. A hybrid approach is common: snooping inside a socket or chiplet where cores share local interconnects, and directory protocols between sockets. This keeps low latency for frequent intra-socket interactions while scaling inter-socket coherence. A misconception is assuming one approach universally wins; the right choice depends on system size, expected sharing patterns, and design constraints like power and hardware area. When designing systems, quantify broadcast rates and directory storage overhead to make an informed trade-off. In practical terms, when to prefer broadcasts and when a directory is necessary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Snooping
Pros: simple hardware, fast reactions on a shared bus. Cons: every cache must snoop every broadcast, causing bandwidth and power costs as cores increase.
Directory
Pros: targeted messages, scalable to many cores. Cons: directory storage, lookup latency, and more complex hardware.
Hybrid approach
Use snooping within a socket or chiplet and directory coherence between sockets to balance latency and scalability.
Key Takeaway

Choose protocols based on system size and sharing patterns: small systems favor snooping, large systems favor directory or hybrid solutions.

screens.title: Hybrid Coherence and Real-World Use
screens.narratorSegment: Many modern multi-socket systems use hybrid coherence: snooping within a socket or chiplet where cores share a fast ordered interconnect, and a directory protocol between sockets. This design leverages snooping's low latency for frequent local interactions while avoiding the cost of global broadcasts. Suppose cores within a socket commonly share data; snooping ensures quick invalidations and supplies. Between sockets, the directory tracks sharers and forwards messages to only affected sockets, preserving scalability. Implementing hybrid coherence requires partitioning coherence domains and ensuring consistency at domain boundaries; that usually means adding a directory that is aware of which socket acts as a proxy for a cache line. A practical misconception is assuming hybrid systems are just the sum of parts; in practice, designers must handle cross-domain promotions, directory updates, and maintain correctness during migrations. For architects, the key is profiling: measure which cache lines are hot locally and which are shared globally, then tune the coherence boundaries to minimize interconnect traffic while keeping latency acceptable. Hybrid systems offer a pragmatic compromise that supports medium to large core counts without excessive broadcast traffic.

Why hybrid?
Hybrid coherence keeps fast snooping inside a socket where a shared bus or ring is efficient, and uses directory protocols across sockets to avoid global broadcasts. This reduces global traffic while preserving low-latency local operations.

Hybrid coherence balances latency and scalability and is common in multi-socket designs.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the core concepts to remember. First, the cache coherence problem: private caches can hold different values for the same address, so coherence protocols enforce per-location agreement. Second, snooping protocols use broadcasts so caches can observe requests; MSI is a simple example using Modified, Shared, and Invalid states to manage ownership. Third, MESI adds Exclusive so a clean solo reader can later write without an extra broadcast. These ideas form the foundation for understanding more complex extensions and scalability solutions. Also remember the scalability rule: snooping is efficient on small buses, while directory-based coherence trades metadata and lookup latency for point-to-point messaging that scales to many cores. Keep these key concepts in mind when reasoning about hardware trade-offs and when interpreting cache coherence traces.

fullNarratorScript:
In multiprocessor systems each core often keeps its own private cache to reduce latency. That speed comes with a coordination cost: if two cores cache the same memory location, a write by one can leave the other holding stale data. This is the cache coherence problem. In this chapter you will learn how snooping protocols use a shared broadcast network to let caches observe requests, how the MSI and MESI state machines control ownership and sharing, and why directory approaches replace broadcasts for larger systems. We'll also look at practical extensions like MOESI and MESIF and a brief hands-on simulation you can run. The goal is practical: you should be able to explain why a read-then-write pattern causes extra bus traffic in MSI and how MESI removes that cost using the Exclusive state. You'll also learn when snooping is an efficient design and when directory bookkeeping becomes necessary. Notice how all these mechanisms trade off bus bandwidth, latency, and hardware complexity. As you move through the lesson, imagine two people reading the same book: when one rewrites a page, the other must learn about the change or discard the page. That simple analogy will guide the concrete protocols we cover and prepare you to reason about scalability and hybrid designs.

By the end of these lessons you will explain why private caches must coordinate and implement basic coherence protocols. Specifically, you will learn to state the cache coherence problem in your own words, showing how a write by one core can cause stale reads in another. You will implement the MSI snooping protocol at a conceptual level and trace its state transitions during reads and writes. You will also describe MESI and explain why the Exclusive state reduces unnecessary bus transactions during a read-then-write pattern. Finally, you will analyze when snooping stops scaling and why directory-based coherence or hybrid approaches become necessary on larger systems. Each objective maps to a competency: explanation, implementation, comparative analysis, and performance trade-off reasoning. Practical practice includes a small Python simulation you can run that models two processors and a few cache lines. These objectives focus on both reasoning about protocol messages and interpreting state transitions in traces, so you'll be ready to read traces, answer design questions, and extend simple simulators.

This companion objectives slide emphasizes applied competency. You'll be asked to trace sequences of reads and writes across two caches and record exact MSI state transitions. You'll demonstrate understanding of bus transactions: BusRd, BusRdX and the idea of an upgrade transaction. You'll compare how MESI introduces Exclusive to avoid needless invalidations and explain MOESI and MESIF as targeted optimizations that reduce writebacks and forwarding costs. Finally, you'll analyze scalability: show why snooping is practical for a small shared bus but creates overwhelming broadcast traffic as core counts rise, and how a directory's sharer vector and owner field enable point-to-point messaging that scales. These skills matter: architecture interviews and systems design problems often require explaining these trade-offs, and real hardware designers use them to choose between simpler fast paths and complex scalable solutions. Practice with the trace tasks and the small simulator until you can predict state transitions and count bus events reliably.

Cache coherence is the property that all processors observe a consistent value for a memory location as if memory were a single shared store. The problem arises when private caches allow one core to modify a value while other cores keep older cached copies. Consider two cores, P1 and P2, both caching address A. If P1 writes A = 5 into its cache and does not update memory immediately, P2 may still have the old value 0 and read stale data. That mismatch breaks the expectation that reads reflect the most recent write. Coherence protocols solve this by defining states and messages so caches either invalidate stale copies or supply the new value. Practically, a protocol must handle three events: a processor read when its line is invalid, a processor write when others may have copies, and requests from other caches for the latest value. A common misconception is to equate coherence with consistency: coherence ensures updates to a single location are propagated, whereas consistency defines the ordering seen across multiple locations. Another misconception is assuming hardware automatically keeps caches synchronized without explicit protocol traffic—snooping or directory messages are the mechanism that enforces correctness. To check your understanding, imagine a read-after-write by different cores; can you explain which cache supplies data and which copies are invalidated? The core insight is that coherence enforces a per-location agreement through state transitions and communication.

Snooping protocols rely on a shared broadcast medium so every cache can observe memory requests and act accordingly. The basic bus transactions you must know are BusRd, BusRdX (read-exclusive), and sometimes BusUpgr (upgrade). When a cache sees a BusRd for a block it holds in Modified state, it must either write the modified data back to memory or forward the data to the requester, then downgrade to Shared. If it holds the block in Shared state, it stays Shared and does not need to write back. On a BusRdX, caches with Shared or Modified copies must invalidate their copies. The typical flow for a processor Read in an Invalid state is: issue BusRd, other caches snoop, if someone has Modified they supply data and become Shared; otherwise memory provides the data. For a processor Write in Invalid or Shared, the cache issues BusRdX or BusUpgr; other caches invalidate. A common misconception is that snooping means immediate coherence at zero cost. In fact, snooping requires every cache to inspect every broadcast, consuming interconnect bandwidth and power. This is why snooping is most effective on small systems with an ordered bus. To practice, trace a Read then Write sequence and mark exact bus events and state transitions; you will see why BusRdX and BusUpgr differ in cost.

MSI is the simplest common snooping coherence protocol. Each cache line is in exactly one of three states: Modified means the cache has the only valid copy and it differs from memory; Shared means the line is clean and one or more caches may hold it; Invalid means the cache has no valid copy. The protocol defines transitions on processor and bus events. For example, a processor read when the line is Invalid issues a BusRd; if another cache has Modified it supplies data and becomes Shared. The requester moves to Shared. A processor write when the line is Shared must invalidate other copies by issuing BusRdX, and then the requester moves to Modified. If a cache in Modified observes a BusRd for its line it must write the updated data back or forward it and downgrade to Shared. A common confusion is the difference between BusRd and BusRdX: BusRd asks for data for reading, while BusRdX asks for exclusive permission to modify, prompting invalidations. Another subtle point is BusUpgr, which upgrades S to M without data transfer when the requester already holds the line. To build intuition, trace specific sequences and annotate which cache supplies data and which transitions occur; this trains you to count writes back to memory and to reason about latency impact.

A small simulator helps make MSI behavior concrete. The hands-on activity asks you to implement caches with three states per line and model BusRd and BusRdX transactions. The given sequence exercises reads and writes and illustrates invalidations and data supply. Conceptually, implement each cache as an array of lines storing state and data. On a processor read when the line is invalid, issue a BusRd and let any M holder supply data then downgrade to S. On a processor write, issue BusRdX; other S holders transition to I, and any M holder writes back then invalidates. A common error is forgetting to downgrade M to S on a BusRd and thus failing to supply the latest value. The example sequence to trace is: P1 Read 0; P2 Read 0; P1 Write 0; P2 Read 0; P2 Write 0; P1 Read 0. When you run the simulator, after P1's write the line should be M in P1 and I in P2; when P2 later reads, it should see the latest value supplied by P1 or memory and transition to S. Extending the simulator to MESI demonstrates how Exclusive avoids a BusRdX for read-then-write when no other cache holds the line. Implement the code, run the trace, and annotate each step with state changes.

MESI extends MSI with an Exclusive (E) state. The E state means a cache has the line, it matches memory, and no other cache holds it. That simple fact yields a meaningful optimization: if a processor reads a line and no other cache has it, the line enters E rather than S. Later, if the processor wants to write to that same line, it can transition directly to Modified without issuing BusRdX because it already knows it is the sole holder. This avoids an extra broadcast and invalidation when the common pattern is read-then-write by the same core. A concrete example: a thread reads a private variable then writes to it; under MSI the read yields S and a subsequent write issues BusRdX even though no other cache has the line, incurring unnecessary bus traffic. MESI prevents that. A typical misconception is thinking Exclusive implies the line is modified; E is clean but exclusive. Also, MESI requires the bus to detect sharers: when a BusRd occurs, caches must confirm whether they have a copy, so the requester can be granted E if no sharers respond. The main trade-off is slightly more complex state logic in exchange for reduced bus events on common read-then-write sequences. Try converting the MSI simulator to MESI and observe fewer BusRdX events in traces where reads are followed by writes by the same core.

MOESI and MESIF add additional states to optimize communication. MOESI introduces Owned (O), which represents a dirty copy that may be shared: the owning cache supplies the modified data to requesters without immediately writing back to memory. This avoids extra writebacks when multiple caches read a dirty block; ownership lets one cache remain responsible for coherence while others hold read-only access. MESIF introduces Forward (F), a clean-state optimization where one cache is designated to forward data to others, reducing duplicate responses to a BusRd. Practically, these states reduce memory traffic and duplicate cache responses but add complexity: you must track an owner or a forwarder and ensure the right cache responds on a bus read. A common misconception is that more states always improve performance; in practice the gains depend on workload: write-heavy sharing patterns may benefit from Owned, while read-heavy patterns can leverage Forward to reduce memory accesses. When extending a simulator, add ownership and forwarder bookkeeping, and test workloads that perform many read sharers or frequent dirty sharing to measure benefit. The core takeaways are trade-offs: more states mean more hardware logic but can save latency and memory bandwidth in the right scenarios.

Directory-based coherence moves bookkeeping to a directory (often distributed at memory controllers) that tracks which caches hold each memory block. A directory entry typically records the block state (uncached, shared, modified), a sharer bit vector, and an optional owner for Modified blocks. When a cache wants to read or write, it sends a request to the directory. The directory looks up the sharers and forwards requests only to those caches that have copies. Another subtlety is directory storage: maintaining a full bit vector per block requires space that can be significant at very large scales, so directory implementations use optimizations like limited sharer lists or coarse-grain tracking. The trade-offs are clear: directory protocols use more complex metadata and slightly higher latency per request but avoid the heavy broadcast costs that make snooping impractical beyond small systems.

Here are the core concepts to remember. First, the cache coherence problem: private caches can hold different values for the same address, so coherence protocols enforce per-location agreement. Second, snooping protocols use broadcasts so caches can observe requests; MSI is a simple example using Modified, Shared, and Invalid states to manage ownership. Third, MESI adds Exclusive so a clean solo reader can later write without an extra broadcast. These ideas form the foundation for understanding more complex extensions and scalability solutions. To close, keep these concise reminders at hand. First, MSI is a basic snooping protocol with Modified, Shared, and Invalid states that enforce single-writer semantics. Second, bus transactions — BusRd and BusRdX — are the mechanisms that drive state changes and must be counted to measure protocol cost. Third, MESI's Exclusive state prevents unnecessary BusRdX after a solo read, saving bandwidth. Fourth, MOESI and MESIF add Owned and Forward roles to reduce writebacks and duplicated responses in particular sharing patterns. Fifth, directory-based coherence replaces broadcasts with targeted messages and scales to many cores while adding directory storage and lookup latency. Sixth, hybrid designs combine snooping locally and directories globally to balance latency and scalability.
